The Edo Consumer Protection Committee (Edo CPC) has rejected a warning by the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) against its enforcement activities.
The committee’s chairman, Osaro Iyamu, disclosed this on Tuesday.
Mr Iyamu’s remark was a reaction to a statement on Tuesday by the NAFDAC Director-General, Mojisola Adeyeye, in which she insisted that the agency is responsible for protecting consumers in Edo State.
PREMIUM TIMES reports that the disagreement stems from the Edo committee’s reported seizure of products, closure of business premises and public pronouncements on the authenticity and safety of regulated goods, particularly Arden Table Water.
In the Tuesday statement, NAFDAC Director-General, Mrs Adeyeye, a professor, warned the committee against carrying out enforcement actions on regulated products without the agency’s authorisation.
But in his statement made available to the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN), Mr Iyamu said the committee had never claimed to act on behalf of NAFDAC, insisting that its establishment by the Edo State Government was aimed at safeguarding consumers’ health and protecting their rights.
“The committee was established by Governor Monday Okpebholo to promote consumer protection and fair business practices in line with the administration’s SHINE Agenda,” he said.

The chairman argued that the committee’s activities were intended to complement efforts of relevant regulatory institutions rather than usurp their responsibilities.
“The committee’s findings during an enforcement exercise exposed negligence by the company’s management toward consumer safety,” he said.
The Edo CPC chairman disputed NAFDAC’s account of the enforcement location, saying the committee operated at Owoseni Street, around the New Benin axis of Benin City, and not in Asaba, Delta.
On Arden Table Water, Mr Iyamu faulted NAFDAC’s clarification that its sachet water registration remained valid, while its bottled water was undergoing renewal.
He contended that the ongoing renewal process did not absolve the company of alleged violations uncovered during the committee’s enforcement exercise.
The chairman further claimed that the company’s management admitted to the alleged offence during and after the exercise, although he did not provide evidence or details of the reported admission.
He also questioned NAFDAC’s position on the use of its product verification and authentication platforms, arguing that the committee’s efforts to encourage manufacturers and distributors to update their registrations supported the agency’s regulatory objectives.
“The committee will continue its consumer protection activities in collaboration with relevant government institutions and organisations,” he said.
Meanwhile, Mrs Adeyeye, in her Tuesday statement, warned that access to NAFDAC’s product authentication platforms, including the Automated Product Administration and Monitoring System, QR code scanners and SMS verification services, did not give the committee regulatory enforcement powers.
The director-general maintained that failed QR code scans, missing registration details or discrepancies in product information were not sufficient evidence to declare a product counterfeit, adulterated or substandard.
She said such observations required further investigation and, where necessary, laboratory analysis before definitive pronouncements could be made.
The NAFDAC official also faulted the committee for seizing regulated products, sealing business premises, and imposing fines without proper authorisation or technical guidance.
“The regulation of food, drugs and related products is on the Exclusive Legislative List, which makes it a federal responsibility,” she stated.
On Arden Table Water, Mrs Adeyeye clarified that the sachet water, with registration number D1-3016L, had a valid registration, while the bottled water, with registration number D1-3065, was undergoing renewal.
She expressed concern over reports that the committee had shut down the operations of Chepfets Mega Investment Nigeria Ltd., the product’s manufacturer, imposed a fine, and arrested without first seeking clarification from NAFDAC.
The director-general said the absence of an updated status on the agency’s NAPAMS portal did not establish that a product was unsafe, ineffective or substandard.
Mrs Adeyeye consequently appealed to Governor Okpebholo to review the committee’s reported actions and direct it to seek clarification from the agency before taking enforcement decisions involving regulated products.
She also disclosed that it had commenced investigations into the circumstances surrounding the dispute, including the reported involvement of its Zonal Enforcement Team in Asaba, and whether any formal working relationship or authorisation existed between it and the committee.
The director-general reaffirmed NAFDAC’s support for consumer protection initiatives and collaboration with state governments but insisted that such partnerships must operate within established legal and regulatory boundaries.
She, however, advised manufacturers to begin registration renewal at least six months before expiration to allow sufficient processing time.
“Traders, distributors, healthcare providers and members of the public are urged to report suspected counterfeit, unregistered or substandard products to NAFDAC rather than act on their own,” she urged.
